scope: Exact arithmetic after blinded key assessments were frozen and final teaching was disclosed. Only the fictional item rates are used; no medical guidance or new model call.
reviewed_explanation_for_50_percent: 50% would require roughly equal true and false positives, which needs ~50% prevalence, not 1/1000.
conclusion: The reviewed 50% distractor explanation is mathematically false. Equal true and false positives require1% prevalence under these rates;50% prevalence yields99% posterior. The item key About9% remains arithmetically supported.

author_record.prompt: A medical test for a rare disease (1 in 1000 prevalence) is 99% accurate: it correctly identifies 99% of sick people and 99% of healthy people. If you test positive, what is the approximate probability you actually have the disease?
author_record.explanation: Out of 1000 people: 1 has disease and likely tests positive; 999 are healthy but ~10 false positives. Of ~11 positive tests, only ~1 is true positive. P(Disease|Positive) ≈ 1/11 ≈ 9%.
author_record.topic: base rates and distinguishing a possible conclusion from a warranted one.
author_record.objective: Apply base rates to interpret diagnostic test results

choices.reason: This ignores the base rate. With 1/1000 prevalence, among 100,000 people: ~100 sick (99 true positives) and ~99,900 healthy (999 false positives). P(disease|positive)≈99/1098≈9%, not 99%.
50% would require roughly equal numbers of true and false positives, which would need ~50% prevalence, far above the 1/1000 given.
1% would be close to the base rate alone, ignoring the positive test result's updating power. The actual calculation gives ~9%.
Bayes' theorem: P(disease|+)= (0.99×0.001)/[(0.99×0.001)+(0.01×0.999)]≈0.00099/0.01098≈9%. The low base rate swamps the test accuracy.
